function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a minimal, production‑ready image for the Node.js app. |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment definition (2 replicas, exposes port 3000). |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Service definition (ClusterIP, forwards to the pods). |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds the Docker image, runs tests, and pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry whenever you push to `main`. |

> **NOTE** – The helper functions you saw in the prompt are only for Python projects.  
> Since this repo is a Node.js app, we’ll hand‑craft the files instead.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Build a lightweight, production‑ready image for the Node.js app
# ------------------------------------
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install only production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this image?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small (~70 MB) and includes the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean, reproducible install.  
> * The image is ready for production – no dev tools, no source maps.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a folder called `k8s` (or `deployments`, whatever you prefer) and add the two files below.

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: "256Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            requests:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "125m"
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What this does**  
> * The Deployment runs 2 replicas of the container.  
> * The Service exposes port 80 inside the cluster and forwards traffic to port 3000 on the pods.  
> * You can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create the following file: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx (needed for multi‑platform builds)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Run tests (optional – replace with your test command)
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm test
```

> **How it works**  
> 1. On every push to `main`, the workflow checks out the repo.  
> 2. It logs into `ghcr.io` using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> 3. Builds the Docker image and pushes it to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> 4. Runs your test suite (you can adjust the test command as needed).

---

## 4. Add, Commit, Push

Once you’ve added the files above, run the following commands from the root of the repo:

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> The workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`.

---

## 5. Quick sanity check

After pushing, verify that:

1. **GitHub Actions** shows a successful run under the *Actions* tab.  
2. The image appears in **GitHub Container Registry** (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`).  
3. If you have a cluster set up, apply the manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

…and confirm the pods are running:

```bash
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
```

That’s it! Your repo now has a production‑ready Docker image, Kubernetes deployment/service, and an automated CI pipeline. Happy coding!
